q: You are about to hoist the mainsail outside the harbour. How do you point the boat?
a: Head to wind, motoring slowly
o: Downwind, so the sail fills at once
Beam-on, so the boat sits steady
Straight for the next harbour
why: Head to wind the sail cannot fill, so it slides up without snagging.

q: When do you put in a reef?
a: Now, before you leave the bay
o: When the boat starts to round up
Once the wind actually reaches F5
Only if the crew start to feel ill
why: Reef when you first think of it — it is easy in calm water and hard in a blow.

q: Your crew pull the sheet to unfurl the genoa. What do you do with the furling line?
a: Let it out under control, a turn on a winch
o: Let it go so it runs out freely
Keep it cleated until the sail is out
Pull it in to help the sail unroll
why: Ease the furling line under control so the sail unrolls evenly and the line does not tangle.

q: You roll the genoa away for the night in harbour. What do you check?
a: Rolled tight, sheets wrapped twice round
o: A corner left out so the sail dries
The furling line left uncleated
One sheet winched tight to hold it
why: A tightly furled sail with the sheets wrapped round cannot unroll in a night gust.

q: Reefing the main, you have eased the halyard and hooked the luff cringle on the reefing horn. What next?
a: Tension the halyard, then pull in the reef line
o: Sheet the main in hard, then the halyard
Tie in the reef points, then the halyard
Lower the whole sail down to the boom
why: Slab reefing: tack down, halyard up tight, then the clew reef line, then the reef points.

q: You are about to reef the main. What do you ease before letting the halyard down?
a: The mainsheet and the kicker
o: Nothing — let the halyard straight off
The genoa sheet and furling line
The outhaul and the backstay
why: Easing the mainsheet and kicker spills the wind so the sail comes down freely.

q: To reef your in-mast furling main, how do you work the two lines?
a: Ease the outhaul under control as you wind in
o: Let the outhaul run free, then wind in fast
Wind in with the outhaul cleated tight
Lower the halyard a little, then wind in
why: Keep some tension on the outhaul as you furl so the sail rolls in tight and does not jam.

q: What do you adjust?
a: Move the sheet car forward
o: Move the sheet car aft
Ease the sheet out further
Unroll some genoa again
why: A reefed genoa needs its sheet lead further forward to close the leech and ease the foot.

fig.title: Genoa rolled to half
lines: Foot of the sail stretched tight

q: You want to stop for a while at sea to clear a jammed line. How do you heave-to?
a: Tack, keep the genoa backed, helm lashed to luff
o: Tack, free the genoa, helm lashed to bear away
Drop both sails, helm lashed amidships
Gybe, keep the genoa backed, helm amidships
why: Hove-to, the backed genoa pushes the bow off and the helm luffs it up, so she lies quietly.

q: You call "Ready about". The crew on the genoa winch is still pulling on a jumper and says nothing. What do you do?
a: Wait for their "Ready" before you turn
o: Tack anyway — they will catch up
Call "Lee-oh" louder and turn
Gybe instead — it needs less crew
why: As skipper you turn only when every crew member has answered "Ready".

q: You are about to gybe in F4. What do you do with the mainsheet?
a: Sheet it in to the centre, then ease after
o: Let it run so the boom swings free
Leave it cleated and turn quickly
Free the kicker so the boom can lift
why: Centring the boom before the gybe keeps its swing short and controlled.

q: The boom keeps lifting and threatening to gybe. What do you rig?
a: A preventer from the boom end to the bow
o: A line from the boom to the mast foot
A line from the boom to the stern cleat
A tighter topping lift to hold it up
why: A preventer led from the boom end forward to the bow holds the boom against an accidental gybe.

q: Tacking about 45° either side of the wind, roughly how far do you sail?
a: About 14 miles
o: About 10 miles
About 20 miles
About 28 miles
why: Each leg runs 45° off the direct line, so the distance is about 10 × 1.4 = 14 miles.

q: Can you sail straight there?
a: No — it lies in the no-go zone
o: Yes — close-hauled on port tack
Yes — close-hauled on starboard tack
Yes — on a close reach
why: The harbour is only 30° off the wind, inside the no-go zone; you must tack.

fig.title: Next harbour
lines: The boat sails about 45° to the wind

q: Each gust heels the boat hard and she starts to round up. What is the quickest fix?
a: Drop the traveller to leeward in the gusts
o: Pull the traveller up to windward
Sheet the genoa in harder
Bear away with the sheets still in
why: Easing the traveller or mainsheet spills wind from the main and stops her rounding up.

q: Close-hauled, the windward telltales on your genoa are lifting and fluttering. What do you do?
a: Sheet in a little or bear away
o: Ease the sheet or bear away
Sheet in a little or luff up
Ease the sheet or luff up
why: Fluttering windward telltales mean the luff is lifting: sheet in or bear away.

q: Hoisting the main head to wind, the halyard suddenly gets very hard to winch halfway up. What do you do?
a: Stop and look up — something is caught
o: Use the electric winch to force it up
Bear away so the wind lifts the sail
Keep winching — it always gets harder
why: A sudden hard hoist means a batten, lazy jack or reef line is caught; look before you pull.

q: What is the safest way round?
a: Tack round through the wind instead
o: Gybe fast with the main eased right out
Let the boom swing across on its own
Gybe with the preventer still rigged
why: In strong wind with a new crew, turning through the wind avoids a violent gybe.

q: What do you do before you turn for the harbour?
a: Reef — upwind it will feel much stronger
o: Shake out a reef for more power
Nothing — the wind has not changed
Ease all the sheets right out first
why: Running, your speed cancels part of the wind; turn upwind and the apparent wind jumps.

fig.title: Morning run
lines: Running at 6 knots before the wind
On deck it feels like a light breeze

q: Which change helps most?
a: Reef the main
o: Roll away more genoa
Pull the traveller to windward
Steer harder and carry on
why: Too much mainsail makes her round up; reefing the main balances the helm.

fig.title: Close-hauled, F5
lines: Full main, genoa rolled to two-thirds
